Premature

pree-muh-CHOOR — starts like 'pre,' meaning before; a premature guess comes before the answer is ready. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Premature is happening or done before the proper or expected time.

Reporters called the election result premature since only half the votes had been counted.

Worked Example

A gardener notices tiny green apples on her tree in early June and picks a few to taste. They are shockingly sour and hard, nothing like the sweet apples of October.

Picking the fruit before it had time to ripen is a premature harvest. Unlike 'wrong,' being premature isn't necessarily a mistake in judgment — it's simply too early.

How Premature Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

untimely

untimely: happening at the wrong or too-early time

hasty

hasty: done too quickly, without enough thought

early

early: before the usual or expected time

Antonyms

timely

timely: happening at exactly the right time

overdue

overdue: later than expected

How Strong Is It? — early → premature → rash

early vs. premature

early vs. premature: Early is weaker than premature — arriving early is often fine or even helpful, while something premature happens before it's actually ready or appropriate.

rash vs. premature

rash vs. premature: Rash is stronger than premature: a premature decision is simply too soon, but a rash one is reckless, made with no thought at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pre-

prefix — pre-: before (Latin)

root — -mature

root — -mature: ripe, ready (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin prae- (before) plus maturus (ripe) literally means 'before ripe.' Something premature happens before it is truly ready — picked before it has had time to ripen.

Use the root in a new word: maturity

Use the root in a new word: maturity: The tomatoes on the vine still hadn't reached full maturity by the end of August.
